children.title: Introduction

blocks.text: The geometry work in Children’s House is sensorial and it offers language knowledge as the children at that age are eager to expand their vocabulary.
The aspects to have in mind are: hunger for words, imagination, orientation and the static geography.
Maria Montessori in chapter 17: “Further elaboration through culture and imagination”
f the Absorbent mind says that the child at this age learns many new words. He has

a sensitiveness for words and he spontaneously accumulates them. If the child it is not helped he will obtain them with effort, therefore it is the guide’s task to facilitate the material “to feed this hunger for words”. In the Children’s House the classified nomenclature is very important and should come in conjunction with the material or experiences in which the children participate.

In the same chapter, Maria Montessori talks about the imagination and the fact that for the world there are no sensorial experiences that can be related to world (the children cannot directly touch the continents or the oceans – everything is of super- size for the child). To aid the children Maria Montessori, made a globe in which the water is represented by smooth light blue paint and the land is made from yellow sandpaper. The globe is an aid to the imagination of the child, to help the child explore something impossible to touch in a sensorial manner otherwise. She continues by saying that the children can clarify their ideas about the world if they are given the correct aid. It is important for the child to use the imagination to discover and understand the world that surrounds him more than just using it only for fairy tales. It helps the child to orientate himself not only in relation with the immediate environment but also with the world.
For children in Children’s House only the static geography is offered to them. They are living in the time of “here and now” and it is not appropriate to offer other kind of geography.
The word geography comes from Greek “Ge” (equivalent of Gaya – for mother Earth) and graphy which was the Greek word for drawing/writing.

Stories of the Nordic flags:
Denmark (White Latin cross on red background 2:3 ratio)

The flag of Denmark is red with a white Scandinavian cross that extends to the edges of the flag; the vertical part of the cross is shifted to the hoist side. A banner with a white-on-red cross is attested as having been used by the kings of Denmark since the 14th century. An origin legend with considerable impact on Danish national historiography connects the introduction of the flag to the Battle of Lindanise of 1219. The elongated Nordic cross reflects the use as maritime flag in the 18th century. The flag became popular as national flag in the early 19th century. Its private use was outlawed in 1834, and again permitted in a regulation of 1854. The flag holds the world record of being the
ldest continuously used national flag.
Swedish (Yellow Latin cross on blue background 2:3 ratio)

The flag of Sweden consists of a yellow or gold Nordic Cross on a field of blue. The Nordic Cross design traditionally represents Christianity. The design and colors of the Swedish flag are believed to have been inspired by the present coat of arms of Sweden of 1442, which is blue divided quarterly by a cross pattée
f gold, and modeled on the Danish flag. Blue and yellow have
been used as Swedish colours at least since King Magnus III's royal coat of arms of 1275.
Norway (Blue/white Latin cross on red background 2:3 ratio)
Fredrik Meltzer submitted his proposal just in time to be exhibited in parliament on 4 May 1821 together with a large number of
ther proposals. It was approved by both chambers during the
following two weeks. Meltzer himself provided no written explanation for his choice of design and colours. However, his intentions may be inferred from an earlier letter of 30 April with his

comments regarding the proposal from the flag committee. That design was divided quarterly red and white. Meltzer objected to the colours because they were too similar to those of the Danish flag. He added that it would be equally unseemly to choose the colours of any of "those states with which we have been or are connected with". Instead, he recommended a tricolor of red, white and blue, "three colours that now denote freedom, such as we have seen in the French flag of freedom, and still see in that
f the Dutch and Americans, and in the Union of the Englishmen".

His eventual choice a few days later of a Nordic cross was clearly based on the tradition established by the other Nordic countries, Denmark and Sweden. This cross represents Christianity. The red and blue colours also explicitly referred to the same two countries, former and present union partners. It was clearly understood by all who took part in the flag discussions locally, in the press or in parliament what those colours denoted. A predominantly red flag had many adherents among those who were attached to the union with Denmark or to its flag, which for centuries had also been that of Norway. Others, who saw Denmark as an oppressor, favored the blue colour associated with the new Swedish dynasty which was seen as more receptive of Norwegian ambitions of autonomy.
Finland (Blue Latin cross on white background 2:3 ratio)

The flag of Finland, also called siniristilippu ("Blue Cross Flag"), dates from the beginning of the 20th century. On a white background, it features a blue Nordic cross, which represents Christianity. The state flag has a coat of arms in the center, but is
therwise identical to the civil flag. The swallow-tailed state flag

is used by the military. The presidential standard is identical to the swallow-tailed state flag but also has in its upper left corner the Cross of Liberty after the Order of the Cross of Liberty, which has the President of Finland as its Grand Master. Like Sweden's, Finland's national flag is based on the Scandinavian cross. It was adopted after independence from Russia, when many patriotic Finns wanted a special flag for their country, but its design dates back to the 19th century. The blue coloring is said to represent the country's thousands of lakes and the sky, with white for the snow that covers the land in winter. This colour combination has also been used over the centuries in various Finnish provincial, military, and town flags.
Iceland (Red/white Latin cross on blue background 2:3 ratio)

Iceland's first national flag was a white cross on a deep blue background. It was first shown in parade in 1897. The modern flag dates from 1915, when a red cross was inserted into the white cross of the original flag. This cross represents Christianity. It was adopted and became the national flag when Iceland gained independence from Denmark in 1918. For the Icelandic people the flag's coloring represents a vision of their country's landscape. The colours stand for 3 of the elements that make up the island. Red is the fire produced by the island's volcanoes, white recalls the ice and snow that covers Iceland, and blue is for the ocean and the sky.
The cross it is considered as the Scandinavian cross.

children.title: Introduction to Geography

blocks.text: In the Elementary classroom the work starts from the whole as this is the most interesting part which can be observed and gradually introduce the details of each cosmic truth. It is more interesting to explore the whole and once the children have grasped the interest, they are prepared to find more about the details, the parts, the effects and the reasons for all of it. This approach it is different from the traditional educational where the education starts with the immediate surroundings and slowly evolves towards the whole.

The children start by learning about the universe with the cosmic fable “God with no hands”, continue learning about the coming of life with the “Story of life”, understanding the connection and the fact that all is an ordered evolution which can give the children a sense of tranquility, belonging and the keys to explore what surrounds them.

Geography comes from Greek: γεωγραφία, geographia, literally "earth description". It is a field of science devoted to the study of the lands, features, inhabitants, and phenomena of the Earth and planets. The first person to use the word γεωγραφία was Eratosthenes (276–194 BC). Geography is an all-encompassing discipline that seeks an understanding of Earth and its human and natural complexities—not merely where objects are, but also how they have changed and come to be.

Geography is often defined in terms of two branches: human geography and physical geography. Human geography deals with the study of people and their communities, cultures, economies, and interactions with the environment by studying their relations with and across space and place. Physical geography deals with the study of processes and patterns in the natural environment like the atmosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere, and geosphere.
The human geography is linked to the fundamental human needs, material and spiritual.

Geography it is present in the daily life of the children and allows them to understand and become aware of the interconnection that exists in the universe, on the planet Earth, in the ecosystem and even in between the human beings. Without this inter-connection it is impossible to function, therefore it lies our responsibility as the most evolved specie to protect this interdependence. The human beings created what Maria Montessori called the “supernature”. A good exercise for the children is to try to imagine our world without the supernature, an exercise of humility but also a way to understand our dependence today on this supernature which evolved to become a fundamental need.

In the study of Geography the children are going to be exposed to a new vocabulary that is specific and necessary to express with exactness the concepts learned. The work with the geography materials becomes as well a work of

enrichment of the vocabulary. Together with the language in the study of Geography the children need to have an understanding of the mathematical concepts of percentages as they may been encountered in many charts to express the proportions.

The geography work from the Children’s House can be thought of as a static work as they learn about the countries, continents – mostly their names, flags and facts. In the Elementary the work can be considered a dynamic work as there is a continuous exploration of the cause and effect.

children.title: General notes on charts, experiments/demonstrations, command cards
Charts

blocks.text: The charts are an aid for the imagination of the child, as in the Elementary the child seeks to explore the whole which cannot be perceive it with the senses.
The charts have to be simple, not charge with scientific facts allowing for the child to concentrate on the main concept.

The charts should not be explained in their totality with the exception with the main aspects leaving for the children to explore the other information. Having the charts numbered helps the children to keep them in order.
There are three types of charts:
Impressionistic
Factual charts
Working charts

children.title: Experiments/demonstrations

blocks.text: The role of the experiments is to help the children visualize how the earth was formed. The experiments offered to the children should be carefully chosen and they should be a key of the phenomena happening on the Earth. It can be said that the experiments are also an aid to the imagination.

The experiments in Elementary are also what the practical life activities are for the children in Children’s House. In order to execute the experiments it is required from the children to use precise movements, a certain order and concentration.

The classroom should have a designed area for working with the experiments, where to store, to dispose the chemicals in accordance to the country’s laws. In the classroom should be also a shelf with the rest of the materials required for the experiments.
The chemical substances in the special cabinet (fireproof and ventilated) should be kept in order with clear labels and markings. The chemical substances should be kept in small quantities.
It is important to have a first aid kit in according local regulations.
The guide should feel comfortable doing the experiments and have a very good knowledge of all the steps.
The older children can help to prepare the experiments so the younger ones are not required to wait for the experiments for a long time.
There are three levels at which we do the experiments:
Impressionistic level – used the arouse the curiosity of the child, inviting them to reflect and draw conclusions
The experiment is repeated this time with the names and the steps. This approach can be more scientific
The children are doing the experiment themselves. The children can use the command cards to do the experiment and in case of dangerous chemicals the adult should be present.

children.title: Command cards

blocks.text: The role of the command cards is to help the children be independent from the adult. The command cards that might be dangerous can have a red outline to mark that it requires the presence of an adult.
The command cards should be coded so they can be easy to use.
The pre-requisites of the command cards are for the child to be able to read and have been presented the experiment before.
The elements of a command card are:
Title
Material
Actual command with a question at the end
Statement on the back of the command card

The child using the command card should first take the command card, read it carefully, gather the necessary material and before starting he can make an hypothesis about the outcome of the experiment. The child can continue with the experiment, observe and at the end write a statement. At the end of the experiment the child can check his statement with the one on the back of the card.

children.title: Story of God Who Has No Hands

blocks.text: “God who has no hands” it is the very first of the fables that we say to the children, they are called cosmic fables, cosmic tales. During the second plane the children are very eager to learn, to understand. The cosmic fables provide the children with a framework which includes knowledge from which the children can choose. The cosmic fables give the children a vision of the universe, these story become a fountain from which the child can satisfy his thirst for knowledge and provide a starting point for the love of knowledge, for the world that surrounds them but also for the universe.

The cosmic fables should always have the quality to strike the imagination of the child, to arouse the interest, we want the child to leave wanting to know more and just then we can provide them with the facts they need. This cosmic fable introduces to the child the immensity of the space but the order as well. The order is important for the humans because the order gives the human beings the sense of security while exploring this vast unknown. The story allows the children to orientate themselves in the universe, to get an image of the Earth in the universe and how it came to be the Earth they know today. Even if the children might have many questions, the most exquisite pleasure for a children is to discover things for themselves, the adult has only to guide this exploration by offering the necessary hints to put the children on the good path.
The second plane child has the imagination as his “servant” to take him on this journey
f exploration and discovery, so necessary for the young mind that is thirsty for
knowledge.

The cosmic fable “God who has no hands” is the most important as it opens up a journey, arouses their interest for the all the future work that they are going to do during the years of elementary school.
The guide should do this story at the beginning of the school year as it provides a lot
f thinking and work for the children. When this story is told all the children can be part

and listen to it, if they heard it before they will understand more and more. The guide can create a sense of anticipation, announcing the story one or two before: “Tomorrow I’m going to tell you a very special story”. In this way the children can prepare themselves mentally for a very special moment.
After the story the children can reflect on the story, revisit the experiments and give them time to talk.
It is essential if the story is edited the important parts of the story not to be left aside.

The children need to be rooted not only in themselves but also in the environment, this extended environment the universe. It is not only important to have the knowledge for the child but also the restless spirit to wonder and curiosity to explore. The child
must have a clear feeling that his is a part of the universe, he has his own place with full rights in this cosmic order.
The story opens the doors for exploration not only in the field of geography but also in physics, astronomy, chemistry, social sciences etc.
This cosmic fable story is thought to be originated in India as a creation of Maria Montessori but the written story was written by Mario Montessori.

Cosmic fable
GOD WHO HAS NO HANDS

From the very beginning people have been aware of God. They could feel Him though they could not see Him, and they were always asking in their different languages who He was and where He was to be found. "Who is God?" they asked their wise men. "He is the most perfect of beings" was the answer. "But what does He look like? Has He a body like us?" "No, He has not--got a body. He has no eyes to see with, no hands to work with and no feet to walk with; but He sees everything and knows everything, even our most secret thoughts." "And where is He?" "He is in Heaven and on this earth. He is everywhere." "What can He do?" "Whatever He wishes." "But what has God actually done?"

"What He has done is all that has ever happened. He is the Creator and Master Who has made everything; and all things He has made obey his will. He cares and provides for them all, and keeps the whole of His creation in the most wonderful harmony and
rder."

In the beginning there was only God. Since He was completely perfect and completely happy, there was nothing He needed. Yet out of His goodness He chose to create and all he willed came into being; the heavens and the earth, and all that is visible and invisible. One after another He made the light, the stars, the sky, and the earth with its plants and animals. Last of all He made man. Man like the animals was made out of particles of the earth; but God made him different from the animals and like Himself, for into his body which would die He breathed a soul which would never die.

Many people thought this was just a tale. How could someone with no hands and no eyes make things? If God is a spirit who cannot be seen or touched or heard, how could He have made the stars that sparkle overhead, the sea which is always astir, the trees, the flowers and the scent they shed around them? Perhaps He could make invisible things, but how could He make the visible world? It is all very well, they thought, to say that God is everywhere, but who has ever set eyes on Him? How can we be sure He is anywhere? They tell us He is the Master who everybody and everything
beys, but why on earth should we believe that?

And really it does seem impossible. We who have hands could not do these things, so how could someone who has no hands do them? And can we imagine animals and plants and rocks obeying God? The animals do not understand when we talk to them, so could they be obedient? Or the winds and the sea and mountains? You can shout and scream and wave your arms at them, but they cannot hear you for they are not even alive, and they certainly won't obey you.
Yes, that is how it seems to us. But, as you shall see, everything that exists, whether it has life or not, in all that it does and by the very fact of being there actually obeys the will of God.
God's creatures do not know that they are obeying. Those that are inanimate just go
n existing, those that have life move and go on living. Yet every time a cool wind
brushes your cheek, its voice if you could hear it, is saying: "Lord, I obey." When the sun

rises in the morning and colours the glittering sea, the sun and it-rays and the water too are whispering: "My Lord, I obey." And when you see birds on the wing, or a fruit falling from a tree, or a butterfly hovering over a flower, the birds and their flight, the tree and the fruit and its fall to the ground, the butterfly and the flower and its fragrance are all repeating the same words: "I hear my Lord, and I obey."
At first there was chaos, and darkness was on the face of the deep. God said, "Let there be light," and there was light. Before that, there was only the deep: an immensity
f space with no beginning and no end, indescribably dark and cold. Who can
imagine that immensity, that darkness and coldness?

When we think of the dark, we think of night; but our night would be like brilliant sunshine in comparison with that darkness. When we think of cold, we think of ice. But ice is positively hot if you compare it with the coldness of space, the space that separates the stars: as hot, you might say, as a blazing furnace from which no heat can escape. Experiment 1(“Colder than ice”). In this measureless void of cold and darkness light was created. There appeared something like a vast fiery cloud which included all the stars that are in the sky: the whole universe was in that cloud, and among the tiniest of stars was our own world. But they were not stars then; as yet there was nothing except light and heat. So intense was the heat that all the substances we know - iron, gold, earth, rocks, water - existed as gases, as insubstantial as air. They were fused together in one vast, flaming intensity of light and heat - heat which would make our sun today feel like a piece of ice.
This raging fiery cloud of nothingness, too huge to imagine, moved in the immensity
f freezing space, which was also nothingness but infinitely vaster: The fiery mass was
no bigger than a drop of water in that ocean of space.

As this cloud of light and heat moved through empty space, little drops fell from it. Just as if you swing some water out of a glass: some of it holds together and the rest breaks up in little drops. The countless hosts of stars are like these little drops. Only instead of falling they are moving around in space in such a way that they can never meet. They are millions of miles from each other.

Indeed they are so far away that it takes the light of some of them millions of years to reach us. Do you know how fast light travels? (The children would answer) 100 miles...200 miles..1000 miles an hour? No, much faster. It travels 186,000 miles, not per hour but per second. Imagine how fast that is. It means in one second it can travel 7 times around the WHOLE world. And do you know how big the world is? 25,000 miles. If we were to drive at 100 miles an hour continuously, all day and all night long, without stopping it would take us more than 10 days to cover that distance. And yet light covers it 7 times in one second. You do 'click' with your fingertips, and it has gone around the earth 7 times already, So, can you imagine how far some of these stars are, that it takes their light 1 million years to reach us?

Then there are so many stars that scientists have calculated that if each of them were a grain of sand, all the stars together would cover up the whole of Ireland up to a height of about 400 meters (England or Alabama 200 meters). One of these stars, one
f the grains of sand among those thousands of billions of grains of sand, is our sun,
and 1 millionth part of this grain is our earth. An invisible speck of nothingness.

One wouldn't think so; the sun doesn't look so big. But that is because it is so far away. The light from it takes about 8 minutes to reach us and if we were to travel the distance at 100 miles per hour it would take us a little more than 106 years to reach the sun. Thus, in fact it is 1 million times bigger than the earth. So big that one of its flames can contain 22 earths. Chart 1a.

When God's will called the stars into being,-there was not detail He had not planned. Every scrap of the universe, every speck which we might think too tiny to matter, was given a set of laws to follow. To the little particles which are like smoke, like vapour - which could only be distinguished as light and heat - moving at a fantastic speed He said: as you become cold you shall come closer and become smaller.. And so as they cooled they moved more and more slowly, clinging closer and closer to each other, occupying less and less space. The particles assumed different states which we call the solids, the liquid and the gaseous state. Everything we know is either a gas or a liquid or a solid, and which of these three states it is at any moment depends
n how hot or how cold it is. Experiment 2 (“Three states of matter”).

Then God gave other instructions. Each of the tiny little particles was given a special love for certain particles and a special dislike for certain others. Some were attracted to each other and some were not. Just like human beings, they like some and refuse to have anything to do with others. In this way they combined and formed themselves into different groups. Experiment 3 (“Power of attraction”) In the solid state, God has made the particles cling so closely together that they are almost impossible to separate. They form a body which will not alter its shape unless
ne applies force. If a piece is broken off, the particles still cling together. If, for

instance you start chipping a flint, the flint and the chips still remain solid pieces of stone. When it came to liquids, God said: you shall hold together also, but not so very closely. So that you will have no shape of your own and will roll over each other. Experiment 4 (“Characteristic movement of liquids”). Thus you shall flow and spread, filling every hollow, every crevice in your path. You will push downwards and sideways, but never upwards. That is why, though we can put our hands in water, we cannot plunge them inside a rock. And to the gases He said: your particles shall not cling together at all. They can move freely in all directions.
But as the particles were also different individuals, they did not become solid or liquid
r gas all at the same time. At a certain temperature some remained solid, others
became liquid and still others became gaseous. Experiment 5 (“Different substances change their state of matter”) And so, while obeying these laws the little drop of nothingness that was to become
ur world, the blazing mass, went on spinning and spinning around itself and sun in the

tremendous cold of space. And as time went on, the outer ring of this mass began to dance, a dance of the elements. The particles that were at the outermost edge became cold and shrank; huddling together they hurried to the earth but as soon as they approached the hotter part they became hot and up they went again. Like little angels they carried a bucket of hot, burning coal into the space and returned with some ice. Chart 3a.

How marvellous it is, and how simple. If you become hot you expand, and as you expand, you become lighter and soar upwards, like a bubble of air in the water. But if you become cold you shrink and fall, as a grain of sand sinks to the bottom of a pond. Because of this law the earth gradually changed from a ball of fire to the earth we know. This was the law that the tiny radiant particles obeyed as they danced their dance; particles too minute to be seen or even imagined, yet numerous enough to have produced the world. For hundreds, thousands, millions of years this dance went on. Finally the particles settled down, like tired dancers, and one after another, they became first liquid and then solid and as they became solid or liquid some of them joined others to which they were attracted forming new substances. The heavier ones went nearer to the heart of the earth and the lighter ones floated above them like oil floating on water. Experiment 6 (“Heavy and light substances”) A thin scum was formed, like the skin which forms on milk when it is boiled and left to cool. It seemed as if the earth had taken some shape. But the elements inside this skin were still very hot and they felt trapped. They wanted to get out. What could they do
therwise? They had to follow the law of God: if you are hot you expand. There was

no place to expand and so they burst out. They broke the skin and it was like a terrible fight. Experiment 7 (“Volcano – outdoor experiment”) The water that formed on the surface turned immediately into vapour and went up as the hot stuff came out from inside the earth. There were also ashes. A veil of cloud was drawn to cover the earth so that nobody could see what was going on. The sun was ashamed of them. Chart 4a.

Eventually the fighting ceased. As everybody cooled down more and more gases became liquid, more and more liquids became solids. The earth itself shrank and became wrinkled like an old apples that has been left in a cupboard. The wrinkles are the mountains and the hollows are the oceans. For, as soon as the rocks had cooled down, water was able to return to the earth and it rained and rained and rained. And the water, being liquid, filled every hollow and crevice it found in its path. Thus the
ceans were formed. Above them was air. The cloud had disappeared. The veil was

withdrawn and the sun could once again smile upon its beautiful little daughter: the earth. Chart 5a. Rocks, water, air: solids, liquids and gases. Today, as it was yesterday and millions of years ago, God's laws are obeyed in the self-same way. The world spins round itself and round and round the sun. And today, as it was millions of years ago, the earth and all the elements and compounds it is made of, as they fulfil their task, whisper with
ne voice: "Lord, Thy will be done; we obey"

Isostasy (Greek ísos "equal", stásis "standstill") is the state of gravitational equilibrium between Earth's crust (or lithosphere) and mantle such that the crust "floats" at an elevation that depends on its thickness and density. This concept is invoked to explain how different topographic heights can exist at Earth's surface. When a certain area of Earth's crust reaches the state of isostasy, it is said to be in isostatic equilibrium. Isostasy does not upset equilibrium but instead restores it (a negative feedback). It is generally accepted that Earth is a dynamic system that responds to loads in many different ways. However, isostasy provides an important 'view' of the processes that are happening in areas that are experiencing vertical movement. Certain areas (such as the Himalayas) are not in isostatic equilibrium, which has forced researchers to identify other reasons to explain their topographic heights (in the case of the Himalayas, which are still rising, by proposing that their elevation is being supported by the force of the impacting Indian Plate; the Basin and Range Province of the Western US is another example of a region not in isostatic equilibrium.) Although originally defined in terms of continental crust and mantle, it has subsequently been interpreted in terms of lithosphere and asthenosphere, particularly with respect to oceanic island volcanoes such as the Hawaiian Islands. In the simplest example, isostasy is the principle of buoyancy wherein an object immersed in a fluid is buoyed with a force equal to the weight of the displaced fluid. On a geological scale, isostasy can be observed where Earth's strong crust or lithosphere exerts stress on the weaker mantle or asthenosphere, which,
ver geological time, flows laterally such that the load is accommodated by
height adjustments. The general term 'isostasy' was coined in 1889 by the American geologist Clarence Dutton

Classification of rocks:

Igneous rock (derived from the Latin word igneus, meaning of fire, from ignis meaning fire) is formed through the cooling and solidification of magma or lava. This magma may be derived from partial melts of pre- existing rocks in either a planet's mantle or crust. Typically, the melting of rocks is caused by one or more of three processes: an increase in temperature, a decrease in pressure, or a change in composition. The chemical abundance and the rate of cooling of magma typically forms

a sequence known as Bowen's reaction series. Most major igneous rocks are found along this scale. About 64.7% of the Earth's crust by volume consists of igneous rocks, making it the most plentiful category. Of these, 66% are basalts and gabbros, 16% are granite, and 17% granodiorites and diorites. Only 0.6% are syenites and 0.3% peridotites and dunites. The
ceanic crust is 99% basalt, which is an igneous rock of mafic

composition. Granites and similar rocks, known as meta-granitoids, form much of the continental crust.[7] Over 700 types of igneous rocks have been described, most of them having formed beneath the surface of Earth's crust. These have diverse properties, depending on their composition and the temperature and pressure conditions in which they were formed. Igneous rocks are divided into two main categories:
Plutonic or intrusive rocks result when magma cools and crystallizes slowly within the Earth's crust. A common example of this type is granite.
Volcanic or extrusive rocks result from magma reaching the surface either as lava or fragmental ejecta, forming minerals such as pumice or basalt.

Sedimentary rocks are formed at the earth's surface by the accumulation and cementation of fragments of earlier rocks, minerals, and organisms or as chemical precipitates and organic growths in water (sedimentation). This process causes clastic sediments (pieces of rock)
r organic particles (detritus) to settle and accumulate, or for minerals

to chemically precipitate (evaporite) from a solution. The particulate matter then undergoes compaction and cementation at moderate temperatures and pressures (diagenesis). Before being deposited, sediments are formed by weathering of earlier rocks by erosion in a source area and then transported to the place of deposition by water, wind, ice, mass movement or glaciers (agents of denudation). Mud rocks comprise 65% (mudstone, shale and siltstone); sandstones 20 to 25% and carbonate rocks 10 to 15% (limestone and dolomite). About 7.9% of the crust by volume is composed of sedimentary rocks, with 82% of those being shales, while the remainder consists of limestone (6%), sandstone and arkoses (12%). Sedimentary rocks often contain fossils. Sedimentary rocks form under the influence of gravity and typically are deposited in horizontal or near horizontal layers or strata and may be referred to as stratified rocks. A small fraction of sedimentary rocks deposited on steep slopes will show cross bedding where one layer stops abruptly along an interface where another layer eroded the first as it was laid atop the first.
Metamorphic rocks are formed by subjecting any rock type— sedimentary rock, igneous rock or another older metamorphic rock—to different temperature and pressure conditions than those in which the
riginal rock was formed. This process is called metamorphism, meaning

to "change in form". The result is a profound change in physical properties and chemistry of the stone. The original rock, known as the protolith, transforms into other mineral types or other forms of the same minerals, by recrystallization. The temperatures and pressures required for this process are always higher than those found at the Earth's surface:

temperatures greater than 150 to 200 °C and pressures of 1500 bars. Metamorphic rocks compose 27.4% of the crust by volume. The three major classes of metamorphic rock are based upon the formation mechanism. An intrusion of magma that heats the surrounding rock causes contact metamorphism—a temperature-dominated transformation. Pressure metamorphism occurs when sediments are buried deep under the ground; pressure is dominant, and temperature plays a smaller role. This is termed burial metamorphism, and it can result in rocks such as jade. Where both heat and pressure play a role, the mechanism is termed regional metamorphism. This is typically found in mountain-building regions. Depending on the structure, metamorphic rocks are divided into two general categories. Those that possess a texture are referred to as foliated; the remainders are termed non- foliated. The name of the rock is then determined based on the types of minerals present. Schists are foliated rocks that are primarily composed
f lamellar minerals such as micas. A gneiss has visible bands of differing

lightness, with a common example being the granite gneiss. Other varieties of foliated rock include slates, phyllites, and mylonite. Familiar examples of non-foliated metamorphic rocks include marble, soapstone, and serpentine. This branch contains quartzite—a metamorphosed form of sandstone—and hornfels.

Rivers usually have two types of origin either through glaciers, they generally are perennial, and rain-fed (seasonal where there are dry spells in a year). Therefore, this will give two types of river origin.

As glaciers melt, the water starts flowing through the least resistant part. Initially this water are in the form of small streams. These forms rills then gullies. As time passes, their path gets deepened due to downward cutting. According to Davis theory, rivers have three stages young, mature and old.

In young stage, rivers are mainly in mountainous region where due to slope, the rivers have huge energy. Therefore, they can carry huge load and participate in erosion. During this stage river is engaged in downward cutting through attrition, abrasion, collision etc. We generally find these types of features: V shaped valley, gorges and canyons, rapids, cataracts, waterfalls and plunge pools, river capture due to headword erosion etc.

In their mature phase, we find that their speed decreases due to reduced difference in the base level and present river level of river. Therefore, the vertical erosion is reduced and lateral erosion predominates. This leads to widening of river valleys giving rise to U- shaped valleys. River cuts laterally and side walls of valley are eroded and plain area starts developing. Its load carrying capacity is also reduced so deposition of large rocks starts in riverbed. General features seen are meanders and oxbow lakes, Alluvial fans and piedmont plains, reduced water divide, leaves etc
In old stage river has lost all erosional capacity and deposition is on peak. Prominent features are sluggish river flow, very wide channel, flattening
f river; water divide eroded away, peneplain, boondocks and delta.
Same applies to river originating due to rain. However, most of them are not perennial. However, general mechanism of formation are same.

Why rain is not salty? Sun puts energy onto the Earth's surface and that includes the ocean surface, and every square metre gets energy at the rate of, on average, about 1 kilowatt, so 1,000 joules per second. This gives energy to the particles of water in the sea and dissolved in the sea are obviously some ions, sodium and chloride, and lots of others as well, that's why the sea is salty. But the water molecules, although they are sticky and they stick to other water molecules because they are what's called dipole molecules, when you give enough energy to the water molecule, it can break the bonds to the other water molecules, holding it into the water, and it can escape as water vapour. It isn't possible to give energy in the same way to the ions, or at least not sufficient energy to make them boil off and get into a vapour state like the water. And this is because they are charged and that charge on them makes them a lot stickier, and they interact with other molecules of water, and other ions in the water, far more strongly than a water molecule does. So, it's far easier for water to escape at the temperatures that we see than those other ion species. They then go up into the air as water vapour until they fall in temperature and this enables them when they also reach a certain height in the atmosphere and interact with other water molecules, dust particles and even dandruff. And they form little droplets, and then you have a cloud. And if you make that air get even colder because for instance, the air has to rise and the air expands as it rises, and the temperature drops, then you get precipitation. The water comes out of the cloud and because just fresh water went up into the air, there's only fresh water to come back out of the cloud, and as a consequence, you get fresh rain. And that's why rivers and streams contain fresh water, but the sea is salty because as the fresh water filters down through the land, it takes a small concentration of salts out of the land and out
f the air too, back into the sea where they slowly concentrate.

They're now at sort of steady state concentrations because if the sea were to become any more concentrated, other chemical reactions would kick in and remove some of the salt, or some of the other things as minerals in a solid form.

blocks.text: With the work with “the fundamental human needs”, the children can see how the humanity if highly dependent on nature. This highly dependence can provide the children a sense of gratitude towards nature. The children will understand that we depend on nature and on human work as well. Introduction of the concept: staple food

blocks.text: The guide invites the child to think about food today. He asks him what he had for breakfast. The child answers. The guide says that both of us have had bread. If bread is such a common food for us, so important so we can call it a staple food.

children.title: Introduction of the folder and the work of the baker

blocks.text: The guide asks from whom we get our daily bread. The guide says that we have a folder with the exact same question. The guide opens the folder and says that it is the baker that prepares the bread. He has on this card a little bread. The card can be an identity card for the baker. What does the baker need to make the bread: flour, yeast, salt and water. He has to knead the dough, lets it rise and when it is ready he bakes it. He works hard, he has to wake up at 4:00 AM in the morning to prepare the bread. We don’t personally know the baker or his family, even so he works for us.

children.title: Introduction of the work of the miller

blocks.text: The guide says the baker needs the miller to get his flour. He takes out the card with the miller. The miller takes the grains of wheat and he grinds them or mills them. On his identity card you can see the windmill. He also sifts the flour to separate it from the husks and the wheat germs. You see the miller works hard to give the flour to the baker. We don’t know the baker, we do not know the miller but they work hard to make our bread.

children.title: Introduction of the work of the farmer and review of the whole chain

blocks.text: The guide continues saying that the miller to grinds he needs the wheat to mill it. He takes it from the farmer. The guide takes the card of the farmer and introduces him – with his icon. The farmer to get the wheat has to sow the seeds, irrigate the plantation, remove the weeds/do some weeding and when the wheat is ready he reaps the field. The reaped wheat are tied into bundles called sheaves and left on the fields to dry. The farmer carries the wheat from the field, has to beat/thresh the wheat to separate the grains from the stalks. Then he has to throw the grain in the air to separate the grains from the stalks. Now he can store the wheat and give the grain to the miller.
The guide says that the farmer gave the grain to the miller, who gave the flour to the baker and who gave us the bread for the breakfast food.

blocks.text: The guide can go through the process with the child. The butcher receives the carcass from the slaughterer. The slaughterer gets the animal from the stock farmer. The stock farmer has raised the animal.

children.title: A3 – From whom do we get our clothes?

blocks.text: The guide can go through the process with the child. The tailor receives the fabric from the fabric salesman/draper. The fabric salesman/draper gets the fabric from the textile manufacturer. The textile manufacturer takes the prime materials from the farmer.

The guide says that we always go back to the farmer and we see the same story of work, transformation done by a chain of humans, all of them working until we get the final product. The consumer it is always the last one in the chain.

blocks.text: The guide asks the children if he collects something.
The children talk about their collections
The guide says that when you make a collection and you have more than 1 of the same piece you find someone else with a collection and you trade one of your pieces for someone else’s.

The guide says that when you trade you don’t use money you just swap it with someone else. This is how it happened many years ago – there were no money so the people traded. If someone wanted a horse he had to find a farmer who had horses and offer to him something that he had. It was a very interesting way of getting your things, this exchange it is called barter. Even today there are still places where people use barter instead of money.

children.title: Tell the story about barter and role play the story

blocks.text: The guide says he wants to tell the children a story
Once upon a time, not long ago, a certain person desperately needed a boat. He asked an Arab who had a boat what he would be willing to sell his boat for.

The Arab said he would only give up his bought for ivory. Ivory was the only thing he needed. Unfortunately for Ali Said he did not have ivory. But Muhammad had ivory and needed cloth. Sadly, for Ali Said he did not have cloth either. However, Ali Said knew another person who had a lot of cloth and need wire. Fortunately for Ali Said, he had a lot of wire. So, he was able to exchange the wire for cloth, the cloth for ivory, and ivory for the boat.
The guide brings the cards with the name tags and the products they have: wire, cloth, ivory and a boat. The children can now role-play the story.

children.title: Conclusion

blocks.text: The guide says that barter was a good enough solution as long as the people where almost self-sufficient. There was exchange even a very, very long time ago in form of gifts. As the people started to specialize and started to produce something in a quantity larger than for the self-use then the constant exchange
f goods started. There were societies like the Ancient Egypt where barter was
used with success for a long time. Barter required people with the same ideals, good record keeping and personal trust.

The guide says then when the people started to develop different habits, tastes, when the people started to migrate it had arisen the need for something different than barter. The people decided to have something else for exchange: money. Introduction of the concept of money and their function: exchange, value

children.title: Introduction of the concept of money and their function: exchange, value comparison, value storage

blocks.text: The guide says that today we want to talk about money. Everyone wants money and money, but why we want it if we cannot eat it, dress with it. There are societies where people do not use money but most of us do. We want to think of money and why we need it – its function
The guide says that we use money in the shops – buying and selling it is done with money. Instead of barter when we go to buy vegetables we can use money – it is a means of exchange.

The guide says that money are used to tell us how much something costs – it shows us how much it costs – it tell us in money not in oranges or cows how much a product costs. It also helps us to compare how valuable is a product compared to the other going through the money.

The guide says that there is another function money has: we can save them. Instead of spending the money we can keep it. Some people save for a “rainy day” a moment in life where something goes wrong.

blocks.text: The guide brings the bowl and says that the money that are collected inside are for the common goods and services. Everyone has to contribute. This contributions are called taxes. f the community.
